unit.title: Production data and concurrency
unit.summary: Own asynchronous work, isolate shared state, preserve stream and network contracts, and build account-aware data boundaries grounded in the active iOS checkout.

lessons.title: Tasks: start work, own it, and ask it to stop
lessons.summary: Decide who owns each task. Start a few requests at a time, keep their results in order, and pass cancellation to the right work.
objectives: Tell apart an async call, a child task, and a Task that needs its own owner.
Use async let for a fixed pair, or a task group for a list; limit active requests and keep input order.
Pass a request to stop through the layers without turning it into an empty success or an alarming UI error.
Name the owner of work started by a screen and the event that asks it to stop.

sections.title: Name the person or screen that owns the work
sections.html:
A task is a piece of work the program can pause and resume. Think of an Android search request in viewModelScope. Which screen owns it? What happens when the query changes or the screen closes? Ask the same questions in Swift. An async function may suspend: it waits while other work gets a turn. Calling that function continues the current task. It does not create a second task or promise a separate thread.

Swift's structured children come from async let and task groups. Their lifetime is bounded by the enclosing scope: it cannot finish while its children remain unfinished. Cancellation of a parent propagates to those children, which must cooperate. This resembles Kotlin's coroutineScope and its children, but do not transplant every Kotlin exception rule or scheduler assumption. Swift has no automatic equivalent of an Android ViewModel's lifecycle scope for an arbitrary class.

In func load(id: String) async throws -> Card, id is an argument label, async permits suspension, and throws permits error propagation. The caller writes try await load(id: "synthetic-7"). Neither keyword promises background execution. Start by drawing the owning task, its children, and the event that ends ownership; performance decisions follow that drawing.

sections.title: Start two independent jobs with async let
sections.html:
async let starts a child task whose lifetime belongs to the surrounding scope, or block of code. Use it when you know the small set of jobs in advance. Loading a title and loading a count can overlap if neither needs the other. Two ordinary await calls instead run one after the other. Kotlin has a familiar shape: start two async children inside coroutineScope, then await both. Compare who owns the children; their scheduling rules still differ.

struct Dashboard: Sendable {
    let title: String
    let count: Int
}
func syntheticTitle() async throws -> String {
    try Task.checkCancellation()
    return "Learning dashboard"
}
func syntheticCount() async throws -> Int {
    try Task.checkCancellation()
    return 3
}
func dashboard() async throws -> Dashboard {
    async let title = syntheticTitle()
    async let count = syntheticCount()
    return try await Dashboard(title: title, count: count)
}

This standalone declaration example needs no UI framework. Sendable describes values safe to cross concurrency boundaries; session 016 develops it. The final expression awaits both bindings and propagates an error. If the scope exits with unfinished children, Swift cancels and waits for them. A child error is observed when the result is awaited; avoid assuming an error instantly interrupts all siblings at the moment it occurs.

The active search parameter converter starts visit-reason and insurance resolution this way, then combines their results with existing search state. Read both the bindings and their later awaits. Optional fallback is a business rule layered on concurrency, rather than evidence that all request failures should be ignored.

sections.title: Use a small work window for a list
sections.html:
A task group holds child tasks for a list whose size may vary. Each child returns a result to the parent. withThrowingTaskGroup(of:) names the child result type through of:; the closure may return a different final type. group.addTask starts a child. for try await and group.next() receive completed results. Completion order can differ from input order. Tag each result with its input index when the final array must follow the original list.

A work window is the small set of requests allowed to run together. With a limit of three, start A, B, and C. If C finishes first, save its indexed value and start D. Do not start ten thousand requests at once. Keep the result array in the parent task, and let children return values. A task group controls child lifetime; it does not make concurrent writes to an ordinary array safe.

In a throwing group, an error that escapes its body causes remaining children to be canceled and joined. If you catch each child's failure and return a Result, you have deliberately selected partial success; document that policy. Swift groups do not directly correspond to Kotlin's supervisorScope. Decide whether one failed item invalidates the entire result before deciding where to catch.

A race between work and a timeout also waits for canceled children before leaving the group. If the operation ignores cancellation, that timeout cannot guarantee an immediate return. Deadlines, transport timeouts, and cooperative task cancellation solve related but distinct problems.

sections.title: Cancellation asks work to stop
sections.html:
Cancellation is a request to stop. cancel() records that request; it cannot kill arbitrary code in the middle of a step. Task.checkCancellation() throws CancellationError when the request is present. Task.isCancelled lets you check it and choose a documented response. Check before costly work, between chunks, and before publishing a result. A long calculation can check without waiting. Merely writing async does not make that calculation stop promptly.

Suspending APIs may report cancellation differently. A URLSession request can surface URLError.cancelled. A blanket catch { return [] } turns canceled work into a successful empty result and may overwrite a newer screen. Keep cancellation distinct in the error mapping and rethrow it. For UI tasks, quiet cancellation is usually appropriate, but silence should happen at the owning UI boundary after preserving cancellation through lower layers.

Use defer for synchronous cleanup that must run when the function exits. It cannot suspend to perform arbitrary asynchronous cleanup. A cancellation handler can cancel an underlying callback operation promptly; its handler can run concurrently with the operation and needs synchronized state. A checked continuation must be resumed exactly once even if cancellation races completion. Resuming a continuation is not itself a cancellation strategy.

Tests should gate a fake request, cancel its owner, release the fake, and prove no stale result is committed. Arbitrary sleeps make this test depend on timing rather than the event ordering you intended to verify.

sections.title: Keep a handle for a Task you start yourself
sections.html:
Task { ... } starts work with a separate lifetime. This is called an unstructured task. Even inside another task, it is not a child whose lifetime the surrounding scope must join. It can inherit actor context, priority, and task-local values: where it may access state, its scheduling hint, and contextual values. Those inherited settings do not pass parent cancellation to it. Returning from the creating function or dropping its handle also does not cancel it. Store the handle when an owner must ask it to stop.

Task.detached is also unstructured and does not inherit the same actor context, priority, or task-local state. It is not a default replacement for withContext(Dispatchers.IO). Choose it only with an explicit independent ownership and isolation design. A detached closure must still capture safe values and may continue after the originating screen disappears.

For a UIKit callback, a stored Task<Void, Never>? can bridge synchronous event handling into async work. Cancel the old handle before starting a replacement and cancel on the lifecycle event your feature defines. deinit alone may be insufficient: a task that strongly retains its owner can prevent deinitialization. A weak capture followed by a strong binding before a long await retains the owner for that await.

SwiftUI's .task modifier has framework-managed cancellation tied to view identity and disappearance. A manually launched button task does not acquire that same lifetime merely because the button lives in SwiftUI.

sections.title: Check again before a result changes state
sections.html:
To commit a result means to accept it into stored or visible state. Mark every await, every new task, and every state write in a loading method. While a request waits, the user can change the query. A cancellation check helps stop unwanted work. A request number checks whether this answer still belongs to the current query. Use both when needed. An old response may arrive even after cancellation, so stopping work and rejecting an old answer are separate protections.

Read the repository converter at its verified anchor, then follow its two awaits. Ask whether fallback should occur only for absent parameters or also for lookup failures. The code's throwing signature matters here. Reading concurrency syntax without reading business decisions produces migrations that compile but change behavior.

For a fan-out loader, define maximum simultaneous calls, ordering, duplicate-ID handling, and all-or-nothing versus partial success. Do not infer fairness or start order from task priority. A task group coordinates a lifetime; it does not provide a fixed thread pool or an API request-rate policy. A concurrency limit also differs from a requests-per-second limit.

Before moving production code, reproduce these decisions with synthetic values in a scratch target. The exercises below contain a worked answer for comparison, but no project feature has been implemented for you. Keeping the experiment separate makes it possible to study cancellation without issuing real requests or editing the existing client.

quiz.question: A parent calls Task { await refresh() } and is then canceled. What is guaranteed?
options: The new task is canceled automatically.
The new task has structured lifetime because it was created inside async code.
The new task is unstructured; cancellation needs explicit ownership.
quiz.explanation: Task initialization may inherit context but does not create the lifetime relationship that async let or a task group provides. Keep and cancel a handle when cancellation should propagate.

quiz.question: A task group loads IDs in parallel. In what order does for try await receive results?
options: Input order.
Completion order.
Priority order.
quiz.explanation: Group iteration delivers completed results. Return an index with each child result and reconstruct the input ordering in parent-owned storage.

quiz.question: A timeout child wins a race and cancels a request child that ignores cancellation. Can the group return immediately?
options: Yes, cancellation kills the request.
No, the structured scope still waits for the child to finish.
Only if the task priority is low.
quiz.explanation: Cancellation is cooperative. Structured scopes join their children; a timeout race needs a cancellation-responsive operation to provide a useful deadline.

exercise.brief: In a scratch Swift target, load made-up string IDs. Keep their original order. Allow at most three active loads, and throw if any load fails instead of returning a partial array.
steps: Define an async loader that returns one String, can throw, and checks cancellation; mark its closure @Sendable.
Return each result with its input index. Start only the first min(3, count) children.
Save each completed value in the parent. Then start at most one next input in the freed slot.
Use a fake you can pause and release. Check out-of-order completion, empty input, and cancellation; name who owns every task.
acceptance: At most three children are active at once and results preserve input order.
An empty input returns an empty array.
An escaping child error cancels and joins remaining work.
Cancellation is not converted into empty success; no production client sources change.
exercise.solution:
The loader below takes a function as its dependency. @Sendable requires safe captured values; @escaping allows child closures to retain the supplied function. The function accepts a String, may wait or throw, and returns a String. Each child also returns its input index. Only the parent writes to output, so the children never race to change that array.

func loadOrdered(
    _ ids: [String],
    using load: @escaping @Sendable (String) async throws -> String
) async throws -> [String] {
    try Task.checkCancellation()
    return try await withThrowingTaskGroup(
        of: (Int, String).self
    ) { group in
        var output = Array(repeating: "", count: ids.count)
        var next = 0
        for _ in 0..<min(3, ids.count) {
            let index = next
            let id = ids[index]
            next += 1
            group.addTask {
                try Task.checkCancellation()
                return (index, try await load(id))
            }
        }
        while let (index, value) = try await group.next() {
            try Task.checkCancellation()
            output[index] = value
            if next < ids.count {
                let newIndex = next
                let id = ids[newIndex]
                next += 1
                group.addTask {
                    try Task.checkCancellation()
                    return (newIndex, try await load(id))
                }
            }
        }
        try Task.checkCancellation()
        return output
    }
}

Each completion frees one slot before its replacement starts. If next() throws, no partial output escapes. Empty input seeds nothing and ends the loop. To test ordering, hold three fake calls behind explicit gates, release index two first, and assert the final array still follows the original IDs. To test the bound, record starts and completions in an actor and check peak activity. To test cancellation, cancel the outer task while children are gated; release or cancel the fake gates so the test itself cannot hang.

This code bounds concurrency, not memory for the final result and not API rate. A production implementation should choose a domain result instead of arbitrary strings and define an error context without logging sensitive input. Compare it with the fixed two-child repository converter: both are structured, but they solve different cardinalities.

simple.story: Mira is making lunch. She asks one helper to wash two tomatoes and another to warm two rolls. Both jobs belong to this lunch, so she checks that both helpers have finished before clearing the kitchen. Then the lunch is canceled. Mira asks the helpers to stop. The helper holding a hot tray first puts it down safely. A request to stop has reached the helper, but the helper still needs to respond. Mira waits for that response before saying the lunch work is over.
simple.meaning: Structured child tasks belong to one scope. That scope waits for them to finish. Cancellation reaches the children as a request, and each operation must cooperate.

example.before: The loader has IDs [A, B, C, D]. Its limit is 3. Requests A, B, and C are active; D has not started.
example.change: C completes with value C1. The parent saves C1 at index 2 and starts D in the free slot.
example.after: A, B, and D are active: still only 3 requests. Once they finish, the output is [A1, B1, C1, D1], even though C finished first.

picture.caption: One completion frees one slot while indexes preserve the final order.

items.label: Start A, B, C
items.text: Three requests fill the allowed window.

items.label: C finishes
items.text: The parent stores C1 at input index 2.

items.label: Start D
items.text: The freed slot accepts D, so three requests remain active.

items.label: Join results
items.text: The parent returns values in A, B, C, D order.

words.meaning: A piece of work that can pause and resume.
A pause while other work can run.
A task whose lifetime is bounded by its enclosing scope.
A request that work stop when it can respond safely.
The largest number of operations allowed to be active together.

simple.remember: Own the work, limit the work, and check before accepting its answer.
simple.boundary: Helpers are people, but tasks are scheduled work and have no dedicated thread. Swift joins structured children; an unstructured Task needs separate lifetime wiring.

lessons.title: Actors: protect state and recheck after waiting
lessons.summary: Use actors to control access to shared state. Recheck old assumptions after a wait, and send safe values between owners.
objectives: Explain actor isolation without assuming that an actor owns a thread.
Use a version check or reservation to protect a rule when an actor method waits.
Keep UI state on MainActor and choose where costly calculations run.
Explain Sendable, @Sendable, and nonisolated; say why unchecked promises do not add safety.

sections.title: Give shared state one guarded owner
sections.html:
An actor is an owner that controls access to its stored state. Its isolated code runs in turns, so two turns cannot change that state at the same time. Isolation means this access rule. On Android you might guard a cache with Mutex. Swift can check many actor access rules during compilation. Each actor instance protects its own state. It does not own a private thread, and a method that waits does not keep its turn for the whole wait.

actor Counter {
    private var value = 0
    func increment() -> Int {
        value += 1
        return value
    }
}
func sample(_ counter: Counter) async -> Int {
    await counter.increment()
}

increment is synchronous in its declaration because its body needs no suspension. The external caller still uses await to access another isolation domain. Inside the same actor, a direct call to that synchronous method needs no actor hop. private limits visibility; actor isolation separately limits concurrent access. These two protections answer different questions.

The call returns an Int snapshot instead of handing out mutable storage. In Kotlin, a suspend function guarded by mutex.withLock could offer a comparable access policy, but Swift's compiler checks many isolation violations directly. An actor does not automatically protect objects it returns if those objects expose unrelated mutable state.

sections.title: An old answer can arrive after logout
sections.html:
Reentrancy means another actor operation can take a turn while the current method waits. Suppose a credential actor starts refreshing account A. While it awaits the server, logout clears A. The refresh then returns. Saving that old token would undo logout. Each state access was protected, yet the account rule still failed. Record a version before the wait and compare it before saving. The protected rule, sometimes called an invariant, is that logged-out credentials must stay absent.

A Kotlin mutex held across a suspending call may block competing callers from entering the critical section; an actor does not implicitly hold such a lock for an entire async method. Avoid waiting for the network while imagining the actor has reserved its state. Record a generation before suspension, then validate it before committing. Alternatively reserve a resource before suspension and define rollback, or make the whole atomic state transition synchronous.

The active credential manager increments a credential index when authentication ownership changes. Its completion method rejects a response whose starting index no longer matches. Logout also cancels the operation and resumes waiters. Cancellation requests stop unnecessary work; the index preserves correctness even if the request still completes.

Read each await as “assumptions about actor state may need rechecking here.” Another actor call can suspend without changing your state, but correctness must not depend on the scheduler choosing that benign ordering. Actor queues also do not promise FIFO fairness as a public scheduling contract.

sections.title: Keep UI changes on MainActor
sections.html:
@MainActor gives UI state a shared isolation rule. You can put it on a class, function, property, or protocol. Callers must obey that rule when accessing protected members. In an app, this actor uses the main thread. Think of Android presentation state on Dispatchers.Main, while remembering that Swift checks a declared access rule as well. Declaring UI ownership makes the contract clearer than repeatedly asking Thread.isMainThread at individual call sites.

This resembles maintaining Android presentation state on Dispatchers.Main, but a dispatcher selection and a global-actor type annotation are not identical features. Calling an isolated async method from another actor requires an await. Code already on MainActor can synchronously call its synchronous isolated methods. MainActor.run accepts a synchronous isolated body; it is useful for a small state commit from another domain, not for inserting an arbitrary async request into the closure.

A Task created inside a main-actor method normally inherits that isolation. Synchronous work before its first suspension can therefore block rendering. await means a call may suspend; it does not guarantee that a large decode or sorting loop moves off the main actor. Use a deliberate worker boundary and return Sendable snapshots.

The repository's SearchServiceModule is explicitly MainActor-isolated. That is evidence about this contract, not a recommendation to annotate all networking types identically. Inspect the called implementation and its executor behavior before drawing a performance conclusion.

sections.title: Send safe values between owners
sections.html:
Sendable says a value can safely cross concurrency boundaries. It is a marker protocol: it sets a rule without requiring methods. A struct made only of safe values can qualify. A struct that holds an unprotected mutable object may not. Declaring that reference with let only prevents replacing the reference; the object’s contents can still change. Check the whole reachable state, rather than assuming every value-type wrapper makes the contents safe.

struct SearchSnapshot: Sendable, Equatable {
    let query: String
    let identifiers: [String]
}
typealias SnapshotLoader =
    @Sendable (String) async throws -> SearchSnapshot

@Sendable applies to a closure or function type; it constrains what that closure can capture and how captured state is used. Sendable applies to the values themselves. Here the array contains Sendable strings and has value semantics. The loader can capture an actor reference that safely owns its mutable state, rather than a naked mutable test counter.

Actors are Sendable references because access to their isolated state is controlled. A MainActor-isolated class can also be safely referenced across domains while its isolated members remain accessible only under the proper isolation. This does not permit a detached task to synchronously mutate its UI properties.

@unchecked Sendable is a manual promise, not synchronization. Use it only when every mutable access is protected by a documented mechanism that the compiler cannot prove. @preconcurrency import can ease integration with legacy annotations; it does not repair a race or make an unsafe dependency safe.

sections.title: Read nonisolated together with compiler settings
sections.html:
nonisolated allows a declaration to be used without entering the actor instance that owns it. It still cannot freely read or change that actor's protected mutable state. A pure formatting helper, which depends only on its inputs, may fit. A getter for changing credentials does not. This keyword changes the access contract. Adding it merely to silence a compiler error can remove a rule that the design needs. Its async execution behavior also depends on language features, explained below.

Keep compiler version, Swift language mode, package tools version, target isolation defaults, and deployment availability separate. A swift-tools-version: 5.9 header specifies manifest and minimum tooling constraints; it does not prove that every target uses the same concurrency checking. This checkout also has Tuist helpers that select Swift 6 for particular package targets.

The executor is the mechanism that schedules a task's next runnable step. Older nonisolated async behavior commonly used a generic executor away from the caller's actor. With Swift 6.2's NonisolatedNonsendingByDefault feature enabled, such a function can stay on the caller's actor. A new enough compiler also supports @concurrent to explicitly select execution away from an actor. Read the effective settings before choosing. Neither nonisolated nor async is a timeless synonym for background work.

For this unit, the minimal examples use explicit actors and stable value contracts instead of relying on a target's default isolation. Before applying an annotation to production, read the target's effective build settings and dependency annotations. Do not turn on a new language feature globally as part of a small data-layer refactor.

sections.title: Decide how long the actor and its work live
sections.html:
An owner is the screen, account, or app responsible for keeping and clearing state. Choose that owner before choosing an actor. A feature cache ends with its feature; account credentials must change with the account. An actor controls safe access, but does not decide who retains it or when its values become invalid. An app-wide actor can safely return the wrong account's data if the design never clears or scopes that data. Memory safety alone cannot enforce the account promise.

If multiple callers share an in-flight task, decide whether one caller canceling should cancel the shared operation. Often the service owns that operation and an individual waiter only stops waiting. Implementing prompt per-waiter cancellation requires explicit waiter management; merely awaiting an unstructured task's value does not forward cancellation from the waiter to the shared task.

Review the credential actor alongside its tests for logout during refresh and concurrent refresh coalescing. The tests use controlled events to establish the relevant interleaving. A successful hundred-run stress test can supplement that evidence, but cannot replace an invariant proof.

Finally, do not claim that data-race safety establishes transaction isolation across actors, disk, and servers. Two separate actor calls can each be safe yet fail to represent one atomic operation. Design a single owning command where possible, and define explicit reconciliation where external systems are involved.

quiz.question: Why can an actor install stale credentials after logout?
options: Actors do not serialize memory access.
The refresh method can suspend, allowing logout before it resumes.
MainActor fixes all credential ordering.
quiz.explanation: Actors serialize isolated execution segments, not entire async transactions. A version or ownership check after await prevents an older operation from committing into a newer state.

quiz.question: A struct has let box: MutableBox. Is let enough to make it Sendable?
options: Yes, the reference cannot be reassigned.
No, the referenced object still needs a safe sharing design.
Yes, provided the struct is Equatable.
quiz.explanation: Reference immutability differs from object immutability. MutableBox must provide safe isolation or synchronization; adding unchecked conformance merely promises this and does not implement it.

quiz.question: What does a MainActor Task guarantee about a synchronous sorting loop in its body?
options: The sort automatically runs on a background thread.
It cannot block because Task is async.
The sort can occupy MainActor until it finishes or reaches an actual suspension.
quiz.explanation: Task inheritance retains the actor context. Async syntax does not move synchronous CPU work away from UI execution; choose and verify a worker boundary.

exercise.brief: Make a scratch snapshot store for a made-up account. Start a load, reset the store while it waits, and prove that the old load cannot fill the cache even if its fake ignores cancellation.
steps: Define an immutable Sendable snapshot and inject an async @Sendable loader.
Let an actor own the cache and a generation number. Save that number before awaiting the loader.
On reset, increase the generation and clear the cache.
Pause the fake, reset the store, then release the fake. Check both the thrown result and the remaining cache.
acceptance: All mutable cache state is actor-isolated.
A late pre-reset response is rejected and cannot refill state.
The test uses event gates and can complete if the loader ignores cancellation.
The solution explains what happens to the waiting caller, not just the cache.
exercise.solution:
This scratch store reports StaleLoad when account ownership changed during a load. That is different from a valid empty result. A screen may quietly dismiss that outcome, but the data layer must preserve the distinction. The declarations below work without a UI framework. The actor owns both the cached snapshot and its generation number.

struct AccountSnapshot: Sendable, Equatable {
    let displayName: String
}
enum StaleLoad: Error { case accountChanged }

actor SnapshotStore {
    private var generation = 0
    private var cached: AccountSnapshot?
    private let loader:
        @Sendable () async throws -> AccountSnapshot

    init(loader: @escaping @Sendable () async throws -> AccountSnapshot) {
        self.loader = loader
    }

    func load() async throws -> AccountSnapshot {
        try Task.checkCancellation()
        let started = generation
        let snapshot = try await loader()
        try Task.checkCancellation()
        guard generation == started else {
            throw StaleLoad.accountChanged
        }
        cached = snapshot
        return snapshot
    }

    func reset() {
        generation += 1
        cached = nil
    }

    func current() -> AccountSnapshot? { cached }
}

load() calls its dependency before committing. While that await suspends, reset() may run. The later guard compares the original generation to the current generation, so the old response is neither cached nor returned as a current success. The cancellation check also rejects canceled callers; it does not replace the generation guard.

This small store permits two concurrent loads in the same generation and allows whichever completes last to replace the cache. That is an explicit limitation, not an actor bug. If “latest requested wins” is required, add a request generation separate from account generation. If coalescing is required, track an in-flight operation and its owner. Those policies should be added only after their caller-visible behavior is defined.

Contrast this worked answer with AsyncCache: its documented invalidation policy allows old callers to receive results while preventing insertion into a new cache generation. Both designs reject stale cache writes, but they deliberately differ in what an old caller receives. Choose the policy that matches the account boundary.

simple.story: A library clerk owns the reservation book. People ask the clerk to read or change it, rather than writing in it themselves. Noor asks for a book, and the clerk phones another branch to find a copy. While waiting, the clerk helps Noor cancel the reservation. The other branch later says a copy is ready. Before restoring the reservation, the clerk checks its number. That number changed when Noor canceled. The clerk rejects the old answer, even though every entry in the book was made by the same clerk.
simple.meaning: An actor protects state access in turns. An await can leave room for another turn. A generation number lets resumed work detect that its earlier assumptions are now old.

example.before: The snapshot store has generation 4 and no cached value. A load records generation 4 and waits.
example.change: reset() clears the cache and changes the generation to 5. The fake then returns snapshot [red, blue].
example.after: The load throws StaleLoad because 4 does not equal 5. The cache remains empty; the old answer cannot undo reset.

picture.caption: Reset happens during a wait, so the resumed load must reject its old generation.

items.label: Load starts
items.text: The actor records generation 4.

items.label: Load waits
items.text: Other actor operations can now take a turn.

items.label: Reset runs
items.text: The generation becomes 5 and the cache is cleared.

items.label: Load resumes
items.text: Its recorded 4 differs from 5, so the result is rejected.

The rule that limits where protected state can be accessed.

A version number for one period of state ownership.
A promise that a value can safely cross concurrency boundaries.
The shared actor used to own UI state in an app.

simple.remember: Safe access does not make an old answer current.
simple.boundary: A clerk is a person; an actor is an isolation mechanism with no dedicated thread. A version check protects one chosen rule, not a transaction spanning disk and servers.

lessons.title: Streams: receive values, keep the right ones, and stop the source
lessons.summary: Follow values from their source to their reader. Choose what to buffer, preserve errors, and give running producers a clear stopping rule.
objectives: Read for await and for try await as loops that may wait for each next value.
Tell apart the AsyncSequence reading rule, an AsyncStream implementation, and a source that starts now or on collection.
Choose a buffer based on whether values replace old state or represent events that must all arrive.
Check bridges for lost errors, demand, early values, and cancellation of the producer.

sections.title: Ask where the next value comes from
sections.html:
A sequence gives a reader values one at a time. AsyncSequence is Swift's protocol for a sequence whose iterator, or reader, can wait in next(). Use for await to read it, and for try await when reading may throw. An Android Flow collector gives a familiar starting point. Still ask when this source starts, whether it repeats old values, and who stops it. The protocol alone does not answer those questions.

func sum<S: AsyncSequence>(_ source: S) async throws -> Int
where S.Element == Int {
    var total = 0
    for try await value in source {
        try Task.checkCancellation()
        total += value
    }
    return total
}

The generic parameter S preserves the concrete sequence type. where S.Element == Int constrains its element, rather than converting every value at runtime. This standalone function can consume many different sequence implementations. The loop is sequential: it awaits one value, processes it, then requests another.

A Kotlin flow { emit(...) } often suspends its producer according to the flow pipeline. That is a useful starting analogy, but the protocol alone cannot promise equivalent producer backpressure. Always inspect the actual Swift sequence implementation before porting a Flow operator or lifecycle assumption.

sections.title: Connect callbacks to an AsyncStream
sections.html:
AsyncStream<Element> connects values produced elsewhere to an async reader. It is one implementation of AsyncSequence. Its continuation is the producer's handle: call yield to offer a value and finish to close production. AsyncThrowingStream can close with an error. This handle can offer many values. A CheckedContinuation, despite the similar name, resumes one waiting function result. Keep the two responsibilities separate when choosing an adapter.

A closure-based stream initializer executes its builder when the stream is created. If that builder subscribes to a notification source or launches a task, production can begin before iteration starts. Do not call such a factory “cold” merely because its return value is an AsyncSequence. Conversely, a custom iterator that fetches only in next() can have pull-driven behavior. Multiple calls to a factory can create independent producers.

Do not treat one AsyncStream as a broadcast channel for arbitrary concurrent consumers. Multicast, replay, and current-state delivery need an explicit abstraction and per-subscriber policy. Sharing one value does not imply that every iterator receives every emitted element. A source intended for one consumer should say so in its contract.

The checkout has both a small stream helper and a networking stream factory. Read where they are constructed and what work starts at creation. A signature alone does not tell you whether retaining an unused stream retains a running producer.

sections.title: A small buffer can still drop values
sections.html:
A buffer holds values until the reader is ready. The usual AsyncStream continuation API has no buffer limit unless you choose one. A fast producer can therefore retain more and more values. .bufferingNewest(1) keeps the newest waiting value and drops an older waiting value. .bufferingOldest(1) keeps the older one and drops a new arrival when full. Choose from the data's meaning. Current progress can replace old progress; a payment command cannot safely disappear.

Limiting the buffer limits queued values. It does not make a callback wait for room. That waiting or demand signal is called backpressure. Here yield returns whether a value was enqueued, dropped, or offered after termination. Inspect that result when loss matters. The reader asking for its next value does not automatically tell an independent callback producer to slow down.

Latest buffering can suit replaceable progress or a current position. It does not suit an ordered list of deltas, booking commands, or an event stream in which dropping one element corrupts the next. Streaming text tokens are often cumulative dependencies, so “keep the newest token” can silently discard part of a response. Instead buffer complete snapshots, bound the transport and parser carefully, or use a channel that explicitly suspends senders and defines cancellation.

Remember that a bounded element count does not bound bytes if a single element can contain an enormous payload. Add payload limits, a policy for overflow, and observability that counts drops without exposing sensitive content.

A deterministic buffering check does not need a timed producer. Create a separate AsyncStream<Int> with .bufferingNewest(1), yield 1 then 2 before making its sole iterator, and inspect the second yield result: it reports that 1 was dropped. Finish the continuation and read the iterator; it returns 2, then nil. This tests queued-value replacement only. Test producer shutdown separately with an explicit stopped signal after the task’s defer; returning from one consumer loop is not itself an observation that the producer stopped.

sections.title: Compare delivery rules before library names
sections.html:
A Combine Publisher offers values to subscribers, the readers that attach to it. Its type names both output and failure. Demand tells it how many values a subscriber is ready to receive. PassthroughSubject does not repeat values sent before a subscriber attaches. CurrentValueSubject keeps a current value with different delivery rules. Combine's values adapter supports async iteration, but do not assume every push source becomes an unlimited queue that preserves all values.

RxSwift's Observable is broadly familiar to an RxJava engineer: disposables, scheduling operators, subjects, and error termination. It does not have Combine's demand protocol. DisposeBag lifetime and AnyCancellable lifetime are resource policies, not equivalents of structured child tasks. Delivering on a main scheduler also differs from a compiler-checked MainActor-isolated API.

This repository's ZDRxCore re-exports ReactiveKit. That is a specific library; do not relabel it RxSwift because its name contains “Rx.” Modern async code, Combine, ReactiveKit, and PromiseKit may coexist at different boundaries. A course comparison can discuss RxSwift while grounding actual repository claims in imports and implementations.

Flow, SharedFlow, and StateFlow likewise have distinct contracts. Port “a current state value with replay and equality behavior” or “a stream of non-droppable events,” rather than selecting an iOS framework by superficial name similarity. Framework replacement without a semantic inventory is a behavior change.

sections.title: A bridge can change errors and timing
sections.html:
A bridge adapts one reading API to another. It can also change behavior. The checkout's Publisher.asAsyncStream() subscribes using sink, offers values with yield, and cancels that subscription when the stream terminates. On publisher failure, it calls normal finish(). The reader sees the sequence end, not a thrown error. That may suit optional notifications. A data screen that must report a failed request needs a different failure rule.

The same file's reverse adapter launches a Task feeding a PassthroughSubject, then returns the publisher. The producer starts before subscribers attach, and the shown adapter does not connect subscriber cancellation to the task handle. Those are concrete review questions about timing and ownership; they are not proof of a production incident. Keep observations separate from claims about which callers experience them.

The networking stream factory provides a stronger ownership example: it retains its producer Task and sets onTermination to cancel it. It also funnels initial request and mid-stream errors through throwing iteration, giving consumers one error path. Still inspect buffering and whether cancellation reaches the actual transport.

A bridge should declare creation time, subscriber count, replay, buffer limit, failure mapping, and stop behavior. If it changes any of these, name that decision and test it. Fewer callbacks in the implementation do not establish semantic equivalence.

sections.title: Stop the producer as well as the loop
sections.html:
Termination means the stream is ending. finish() prevents further production, but the reader can still receive values already buffered. Canceling a consumer that is waiting can trigger termination cleanup. Simply breaking out of a loop is different. Other references may still keep the stream and its producer alive. If leaving early must promptly stop an external resource, provide an explicit stop handle. Then test that the source stopped; seeing the loop return is only evidence about the reader.

onTermination is a Sendable callback that can run outside the UI's isolation. It should perform safe cleanup, such as canceling a task, rather than directly mutating a label or view model. If cleanup needs actor state, design an asynchronous hop carefully and account for its new unstructured lifetime. Prefer a producer that owns its resource and can close it without involving presentation code.

A useful test creates the stream before collection, generates more values than its buffer, then collects. A second test cancels while awaiting a value. A third stops after the first received value. Count producer starts, drops, and stops independently. Also distinguish an upstream error from normal completion.

Streams that never finish are legitimate for long-lived observation, but only when their owner and teardown are explicit. Infinite observation retained by a screen can keep both the screen and a resource alive indefinitely.

quiz.question: Does AsyncSequence guarantee a cold, multicast, lossless source?
options: Yes, all iterators receive all values.
No, it specifies async iteration; the implementation defines those behaviors.
Yes, if the Element is Sendable.
quiz.explanation: AsyncSequence provides the iterator interface. Production timing, fan-out, replay, buffering, and lifetime remain part of the particular sequence's contract.

quiz.question: What happens when a continuation yields into a full bufferingNewest(1) queue?
options: The producer suspends until the consumer catches up.
An older buffered value can be dropped while the newest value is retained.
The consumer automatically throws.
quiz.explanation: Continuation yield is not a suspending send. A bounded buffering policy limits retention by dropping values; the producer must handle its yield result if loss matters.

quiz.question: Why is mapping Publisher failure to continuation.finish() potentially wrong?
options: AsyncStream always rethrows the original publisher error.
It turns an upstream error into normal completion.
finish always cancels the consumer's parent.
quiz.explanation: Plain AsyncStream cannot represent a thrown upstream failure. Use AsyncThrowingStream or an explicit error element when consumer behavior depends on that failure.

exercise.brief: Create a made-up progress stream for one reader. Keep only the newest waiting value, and provide a stop action that works when the reader leaves early. Keep UI code out of it.
steps: Create an AsyncStream and its continuation with bufferingNewest(1).
Start one owned task that emits integer progress and uses sleep that responds to cancellation.
Cancel that task on termination. Also return a stop closure for an early exit.
Read one value, then stop in defer. In a separate check, offer values before reading and verify which value is dropped.
acceptance: The contract permits dropped progress and excludes ordered event deltas.
The producer checks termination and always finishes on exit.
A consumer that breaks early can explicitly stop production.
The test distinguishes dropped values, normal finish, and canceled work.
exercise.solution:
The example below uses Foundation and makeStream, available on iOS 17 and the matching modern platforms. It returns a stream plus an explicit stop closure. That closure holds a task handle whose cancellation is safe. The buffer allows one waiting value; the reader can also already be processing a value. Nanosecond sleep gives the producer a wait that responds to cancellation.

import Foundation

func progressStream() -> (
    stream: AsyncStream<Int>,
    stop: @Sendable () -> Void
) {
    let (stream, continuation) = AsyncStream<Int>.makeStream(
        bufferingPolicy: .bufferingNewest(1)
    )
    let task = Task {
        defer { continuation.finish() }
        do {
            for value in 0...10 {
                try Task.checkCancellation()
                switch continuation.yield(value) {
                case .terminated:
                    return
                case .dropped, .enqueued:
                    break
                @unknown default:
                    break
                }
                try await Task.sleep(nanoseconds: 10_000_000)
            }
        } catch {
            // Progress cancellation is quiet completion by contract.
        }
    }
    continuation.onTermination = { _ in task.cancel() }
    return (stream, { task.cancel() })
}

func observeFirstProgress() async -> Int? {
    let (stream, stop) = progressStream()
    defer { stop() }
    for await value in stream {
        return value
    }
    return nil
}

The producer's defer closes the stream on normal completion, cancellation, or termination. The consumer's defer explicitly cancels on early return even if it still holds a stream reference. This example intentionally treats producer cancellation as normal completion because progress is advisory; a request-result stream should preserve its failure contract instead.

The dropped branch currently accepts loss. In an instrumented exercise, count drops in an actor or another synchronized metric collector. Do not spawn one task per drop, since that can create an unbounded backlog outside the bounded stream. A later requirement for every update would demand a different producer-consumer protocol, not merely a larger magic buffer size.

lessons.title: Requests: check the response, decode it, and retry safely
lessons.summary: Keep network delivery, HTTP status, JSON shape, cancellation, and account credentials separate. Retry only when repeating the operation is safe.
objectives: Check HTTP status before decoding, and keep it separate from transport failure.
Explain how the endpoint treats a missing key, null, and a value of the wrong type.
Attach credentials at the trusted request boundary and decide who owns a shared refresh.
Set retry limits, respond to cancellation, and explain when repetition can duplicate an operation.

sections.title: Receiving a response does not mean success
sections.html:
Transport is the work of sending bytes and receiving a response. An HTTP status describes how the server handled the request. Just as with OkHttp, successful delivery can still bring a 404 or 500. URLSession handles transport; JSONDecoder turns JSON bytes into values. Neither decides your product's success, account access, retries, or message to the user. Treat these as separate decisions so a server rejection is not mistaken for bad JSON or a broken connection.

Separate request construction, credential adaptation, transport, HTTP validation, decoding, domain mapping, and caching. A small injectable transport protocol lets tests supply bytes and responses without hitting a server. A repository can depend on the protocol while app composition provides the real session and any interception required by the product.

The active URLSessionDispatcher injects a URLSessionDataTaskProvider; its documentation assigns request interception to app composition. This is an actual boundary in the checkout, not permission to bypass interception with URLSession.shared in a feature. The learning examples use synthetic endpoints and fakes; production requests must go through the approved client configuration.

Write the failure taxonomy before the implementation. A canceled operation, an offline transport, an HTTP rejection, and malformed successful JSON need different recovery decisions even if each eventually becomes one UI error state.

sections.title: Read both the bytes and the response
sections.html:
URLRequest describes what to send: URL, method, headers, body, and timeout. URLComponents builds the parts of a URL, and query items represent named query values. Use them instead of joining raw user text onto a URL. Query values and path segments have different encoding rules. setValue replaces a header value; addValue appends another value. A bearer Authorization header normally needs replacement, not an accidental list of credentials.

try await session.data(for: request) returns (Data, URLResponse). for: is an argument label, while tuple destructuring names the two results locally. Cast the response to HTTPURLResponse before inspecting status. The data method generally buffers the response body; for incremental processing inspect the bytes API and the sequence's ownership. Async URLSession APIs require an appropriate deployment target, commonly iOS 15 or later.

A JSON-bearing 200 response, a successful empty 204, and a cache-validation 304 are different contracts. Do not indiscriminately decode every successful response into the same model. HTTP caches may process conditional responses before your consumer sees them, so integrate application freshness rules with session cache policy rather than inventing a second independent cache.

Preserve CancellationError and transport cancellation such as URLError.cancelled. The repository dispatcher shows both special cases before mapping offline failures. A broad error transformation can otherwise turn navigation cancellation into an alarming connectivity message.

sections.title: Decode the shape the endpoint actually sends
sections.html:
Decoding turns bytes into typed values. Decodable describes a type that can be read this way; Encodable describes one that can be written. Codable combines both. A response that is never written may need only Decodable. Swift can generate decoding for stored properties. A nested CodingKeys enum names or renames the JSON fields. A DTO is a data transfer object: a value shaped for the endpoint rather than every use in the app.

struct CardDTO: Decodable, Sendable {
    let id: String
    let title: String
    let subtitle: String?
    enum CodingKeys: String, CodingKey {
        case id
        case title = "display_title"
        case subtitle
    }
}

String? permits absence or JSON null under synthesized optional decoding. A number where a string is expected still throws; optionality is not permissive type coercion. A default stored-property value does not reliably provide your intended “missing key” decoding behavior. Write an explicit initializer when fallback is part of the schema.

Choose key and date strategies deliberately. Automatic snake-case conversion is convenient but can be surprising around acronyms and manual CodingKeys. Date strategies do not make every timestamp format equivalent; fractional seconds and timezone rules need fixture coverage. New unknown object keys are usually ignored, while an enum receiving an unknown raw value can fail decoding. Compatibility policy must be explicit rather than accomplished by turning every field optional.

sections.title: Missing and null can mean different changes
sections.html:
A missing key is absent from a JSON object. A null key is present with an explicit empty value. decodeIfPresent returns nil for either case. That is often useful for display data. A patch, or partial update, may instead mean “keep the note” when missing and “clear the note” when null. First use contains to check presence, then decodeNil to check null. A number supplied for a required string must still fail.

enum FieldChange: Sendable, Equatable {
    case omitted
    case clear
    case set(String)
}
struct NoteChange: Decodable, Sendable {
    let note: FieldChange
    enum CodingKeys: String, CodingKey { case note }

    init(from decoder: any Decoder) throws {
        let box = try decoder.container(keyedBy: CodingKeys.self)
        if !box.contains(.note) {
            note = .omitted
        } else if try box.decodeNil(forKey: .note) {
            note = .clear
        } else {
            note = .set(try box.decode(String.self, forKey: .note))
        }
    }
}

The leading dot uses contextual type inference for enum cases and CodingKeys. This standalone model intentionally decodes only; encoding a patch needs the matching explicit policy: omit the key, encode nil, or encode the string. Synthesized encoding of a normal optional often omits nil keys, so it cannot silently stand in for a clear command.

Keep fixtures for {}, {"note":null}, {"note":"synthetic"}, and {"note":7}. The last fixture proves the distinction does not accidentally accept malformed data.

sections.title: Let the account owner attach and refresh tokens
sections.html:
A bearer token is a secret used to identify an authorized session. Attach it only to allowed HTTPS hosts and intended endpoints. A feature's chosen URL is not enough proof of trust. Define what happens on redirects, alternate hosts, and existing Authorization headers. URLSession authentication challenges handle transport authentication; adding an OAuth bearer header is a different operation. Keep the token out of URL queries, logs, analytics, and snapshots so diagnostics do not become a second place to expose it.

The credential actor in this checkout checks a trusted-domain predicate, HTTPS, and whether Authorization already exists before adding a token. It coalesces authentication work and uses a credential index to reject stale completion. Inspect its preconditions rather than teaching “every 401 triggers refresh.” A refresh endpoint must avoid recursively triggering the same credential adaptation or refresh path.

Multiple callers failing together should not initiate a refresh storm. The account service usually owns one refresh, while callers wait for its outcome. A caller's cancellation and logout are different: an individual canceled screen should not necessarily cancel refresh needed by other screens; logout invalidates account ownership and must prevent any old result from restoring credentials.

Allow at most the documented number of refresh attempts per request. Refresh failure may mean expired authorization, a temporary transport failure, or a server policy rejection. Do not reduce all three to an automatic retry loop or an unconditional logout without the endpoint's actual contract.

sections.title: Check whether doing it twice changes the result
sections.html:
An operation is idempotent when repeating it has the same intended effect as doing it once. A read-only GET often fits. A booking POST may create a booking even if the response is lost. Repeating it can create another booking. An idempotency key is a server-supported identifier for the one logical operation. Keep that key the same across attempts when the server contract supports it. A new key for each attempt can make every replay look like a new operation.

Bound retries with both a maximum attempt count and a total time limit. Increasing delays can reduce repeated load; jitter adds a small random spread so callers do not all retry together. Waiting must respond to cancellation. Read a valid Retry-After under the endpoint's policy. Codes such as 429 or 503 are reasons to evaluate that policy. Repeating malformed JSON or a validation failure usually cannot fix the contract or code that caused it.

A request body must also be replayable. A consumed stream, signed request, expiring token, or one-time nonce may require rebuilding the request. Attach freshly adapted credentials after refresh while preserving the logical request identity. Test maximum attempts and cancellation during delay; never swallow cancellation and then schedule another attempt.

The active app constructs both the existing dispatcher and an alternate URLSession dispatcher, with selection managed elsewhere. This lesson explains the transport boundary; it does not claim the whole application has already migrated. Preserve request hooks, cookies, TLS configuration, interception, and tracing when comparing transports.

quiz.explanation: Client uncertainty does not prove server failure. Replays need the endpoint's supported idempotency semantics; using a new key can create a new operation.

exercise.solution:
The Foundation client below receives its transport from the caller. A fake can supply response bytes without a server. UI code never needs to decode them, and the client never picks a global URLSession. This endpoint expects a JSON body on success. A 204 means no content, so this particular client rejects it rather than trying to decode an absent card.

import Foundation

protocol CardTransport: Sendable {
    func data(for request: URLRequest) async throws -> (Data, URLResponse)
}
struct Card: Sendable, Equatable {
    let id: String
    let title: String
    let subtitle: String?
}
enum CardReadError: Error {
    case nonHTTP
    case status(Int)
    case emptyRepresentation
}
struct CardClient: Sendable {
    let transport: any CardTransport

    func read(_ request: URLRequest) async throws -> Card {
        try Task.checkCancellation()
        let (data, response) = try await transport.data(for: request)
        try Task.checkCancellation()
        guard let http = response as? HTTPURLResponse else {
            throw CardReadError.nonHTTP
        }
        guard (200...299).contains(http.statusCode) else {
            throw CardReadError.status(http.statusCode)
        }
        guard http.statusCode != 204, !data.isEmpty else {
            throw CardReadError.emptyRepresentation
        }
        let dto = try JSONDecoder().decode(CardDTO.self, from: data)
        return Card(id: dto.id, title: dto.title, subtitle: dto.subtitle)
    }
}

any CardTransport stores an existential dependency: a value conforming to the protocol whose concrete type can vary. The protocol's Sendable requirement makes that dependency safe to carry with this client across isolation domains. The local decoder avoids concurrently mutating shared decoder configuration.

A fixture with status 401 and malformed bytes must yield the status error, proving HTTP validation precedes decoding. A 200 with a numeric title must yield a decoding error. A transport throwing cancellation must keep that cancellation observable. Use https://example.invalid/cards/synthetic-1 only to construct request and response metadata for a fake; do not send it over the network.

This minimal client deliberately has no refresh or retry implementation. Its worked boundary makes those policies testable additions rather than accidental generic behavior. In a production adapter, inject the repository's approved transport, define response size and content-type constraints, and put account refresh policy in its established owner.

lessons.title: Storage and dependencies: choose owners before tools
lessons.summary: Choose storage from what the data promises: a preference, a rebuildable cache, a lasting draft, or a secret. Pass dependencies with clear account and lifetime rules.
objectives: Tell apart preferences, caches, lasting user work, and credentials.
Define which account owns data, what logout clears, and how old stored formats are upgraded.
Use protocols to state behavior and isolation, then pass implementations with a clear lifetime.
Read ZDModules and Swinject as real boundaries; explain why dependency injection does not supply thread safety.

sections.title: Ask who owns each value and whether it may be lost
sections.html:
Persistence means keeping data beyond the current process. Before picking a store, ask who owns each value and whether losing it is acceptable. An Android preference, Room draft, HTTP cache, and credential already make different promises. On iOS, start with those same questions. Can you rebuild the value? Is it the only copy of someone's work? Is it sensitive? What should happen on logout or a read failure? “Save this object” does not answer any of those questions.

A cache can usually be discarded and rebuilt. A draft may be the only copy of a user's work. Preferences influence behavior but should not become a hidden database. Credentials authorize access and require a security-specific store. Placing them all in one convenience JSON file makes backup, deletion, and error handling harder to explain.

Account ownership is distinct from persistence mechanism. An in-memory dictionary shared across accounts can leak prior account data even though nothing is written to disk. An encrypted database can make the same mistake if queries omit account scope. Include account identity or a scoped store instance in the contract, and invalidate pending work when that identity changes.

Decide what logout clears, what can remain as non-sensitive public cache, and what a late operation is allowed to commit. A task finishing after logout must not recreate the deleted account cache or credential. This is a cross-layer ownership rule rather than a storage API option.

sections.title: Match the store to the promise
sections.html:
UserDefaults keeps small preferences, such as whether a made-up tutorial is hidden. A preference is a setting, not a secret or a table of user records. UserDefaults does not promise that several keys change together as one transaction. A getter that returns false or zero can hide the difference between “never saved” and “saved as false or zero.” Registered defaults supply fallback values; they are not the same as values actually persisted by the user.

Files work well for bounded serialized snapshots when you define schema versioning, atomic replacement, error behavior, and backup policy. Cache directories can be purged by the system; do not store irreplaceable drafts there. Application Support and Documents serve different purposes. A sandbox limits access by other apps, but does not remove the need to choose data protection and backup exclusions according to sensitivity.

For richer relationships and queries, Core Data manages object graphs and persistence; SwiftData offers a newer model API on supported platforms, including iOS 17+. Neither is a line-for-line Room replacement. Core Data managed object contexts have queue confinement rules, and SwiftData model contexts require appropriate isolation. Do not pass live managed objects across arbitrary tasks; pass stable IDs or immutable snapshots and refetch in the destination context.

A repository actor can own a store adapter, but that actor does not automatically override the underlying framework's context or queue rules. Preserve both layers' constraints. Model migration, transaction boundaries, and recovery from corruption deserve fixture-backed decisions before shipping an updated schema.

sections.title: Choose when a Keychain secret may be read
sections.html:
The Keychain stores small secrets such as session tokens under access rules. A secret's identity includes its item class and attributes such as service and account. Access groups control sharing; accessibility controls when access is possible. Synchronization is another setting. These choices affect both lookup and lifetime. Calls return OSStatus, a result code. Missing, duplicate, denied, and temporarily unavailable items need different responses. A failed read does not automatically mean the account has no credential.

WhenUnlocked limits access to unlocked-device periods. AfterFirstUnlock may fit some background work but offers a different access window. A ThisDeviceOnly variant prevents migration of the item to another device through backup restore; it does not by itself define iCloud synchronization or every lifetime property. Accessibility is also different from requiring user authentication for each access.

The active credential storage sets kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked, which can migrate with encrypted backups. Teach that observed policy accurately; do not silently describe it as ThisDeviceOnly. A product's background-refresh and account-security needs determine whether a different policy is appropriate.

Do not depend on app uninstall reliably clearing Keychain items or on universal reinstall persistence. Define account reset and credential deletion deliberately and verify supported device behavior. Disk cleanup and Keychain cleanup are separate operations. Never print the token while diagnosing a failed delete, and test errors using fakes rather than real account secrets.

sections.title: Use a protocol to state a real promise
sections.html:
A protocol lists the operations an implementation must provide. Swift structs, classes, and actors can conform when their access rules fit those operations. An actor cannot satisfy any ordinary synchronous requirement by freely reading protected state from outside. An async requirement gives a caller a place to wait for actor entry. A @MainActor protocol can instead state that a UI capability belongs to the UI actor. Describe behavior and isolation together so callers know what they may ask.

struct StoredCard: Codable, Sendable, Equatable {
    let id: String
    let title: String
}
protocol CardStore: Sendable {
    func read(for accountID: String) async throws -> [StoredCard]
    func replace(_ cards: [StoredCard], for accountID: String) async throws
    func clear(for accountID: String) async throws
}

The first parameter of replace has no external label because of _; the account uses the explicit label for:. The protocol requires Sendable because consumers may hold it across isolation domains. It does not promise a particular database or silently require UI isolation.

any CardStore holds a value conforming to CardStore while hiding its concrete implementation. Swift calls this an existential. A generic T: CardStore instead keeps the concrete type in the function's type information. Choose the form that helps your boundary and tests. A protocol earns its place when callers need a genuine replacement or ownership boundary, not merely because every helper in an Android template had an interface.

sections.title: Pass dependencies where their lifetime is chosen
sections.html:
Dependency injection, or DI, means giving an object the collaborators it needs. Constructor injection passes them when that object is created. The composition root is the place that chooses real implementations and lifetimes: app, account, feature, or request. An Android DI component may express those scopes. In Swift you can construct objects directly or use a container. Either way, decide who keeps each dependency alive and who clears it when its owner ends.

The active DIContainer aliases Swinject's Container. Its set(value:for:) helper registers container-scoped instances. Its child-container helper explicitly says the caller must retain the child. Those are concrete retention choices. A singleton registration does not make a mutable service Sendable, and a DI container is not an isolation domain just because many dependencies pass through it.

Resolve the correct protocol type at composition, then pass it to the feature. Registering a concrete type when consumers resolve a protocol can produce missing dependencies or unintended fallback instances. The helper's generic default type is convenient, so inspect call sites that explicitly use for:. Silent fallback creation can also accidentally bypass account-scoped configuration.

Prefer tests that inject an in-memory actor store over tests that share a global container. The fake should preserve cancellation, account scope, and error semantics relevant to the test. A fake that always returns success cannot establish that a persistence failure is handled correctly.

sections.title: Read the shared module as it exists today
sections.html:
ZDModules is the checkout's shared home for contracts used across features and their related models. Its SearchServiceModule declares MainActor ownership and an async search that can throw. Its AuthModule also exposes navigation types and imports UIKit. Those are actual public promises, not a fully platform-independent domain layer. Read the signatures and dependencies before moving another type there. A shared module should make the needed boundary clear rather than collect every useful helper.

A shared contract should avoid forcing one feature to import another feature's concrete implementation. It can still intentionally expose platform capabilities where coordination requires them. Review the Package.swift dependencies and public signatures together: an interface-only intention can be weakened by adding heavyweight shared types or feature-specific implementation details.

When adding a hypothetical store boundary, decide whether it belongs in a feature, infrastructure, or a shared contract module based on real consumers. Do not place everything in ZDModules to make it discoverable. Avoid circular dependencies, unnecessary public surface, and protocols carrying raw decoder or database-context types into UI code.

Migration should preserve current callers while a new adapter is introduced. Document store schema, account scope, and fallback behavior alongside the protocol. A renamed interface is not an architecture improvement if it still hides a global, returns unsafe live objects, or loses cancellation. The next lab composes these decisions with a request pipeline.

quiz.question: A Keychain read returns a protected-data availability error. What should the store infer?
options: The credential is definitely absent.
The read failed under current conditions; absence requires its own status.
The token must be copied into UserDefaults.
quiz.explanation: Availability and missing-item outcomes are different. Treating all errors as absence can cause incorrect login or overwrite behavior and hides the real storage condition.

quiz.question: Does registering one instance in Swinject's container make its mutable state safe across tasks?
options: Yes, singleton scope supplies a lock.
No, retention scope and concurrency isolation are separate contracts.
Yes, if the service has a protocol.
quiz.explanation: The container decides which instance callers receive. The instance still needs actor isolation, immutable values, or another correct synchronization design.

quiz.question: Why should a data protocol return snapshots rather than arbitrary live Core Data objects?
options: Snapshots remove all storage errors.
Live objects have context and queue constraints; snapshots can be designed for safe transfer.
Core Data can never be used in async code.
quiz.explanation: Context confinement remains relevant under concurrency. Pass stable IDs or Sendable value snapshots and use the appropriate context to access managed state.

exercise.brief: Build an in-memory CardStore for made-up accounts in a scratch target. Pass it to a made-up feature. Explain what a disk adapter would still need before it can promise durable storage.
steps: Reuse StoredCard and CardStore from the lesson.
Keep a dictionary inside an actor, with a separate entry for each made-up account ID.
Create the feature with an explicit any CardStore dependency. Do not look up a global container inside its methods.
Write different cards for A and B. Clear A and check that B remains; explain why one replacement does not suspend halfway through.
Describe stored-format upgrades, locked-device access, transactions, backup, and read/write failures for a future durable adapter.
acceptance: Account identity is required for every storage operation.
The fake safely crosses task boundaries without unchecked Sendable.
The dependency lifetime is visible at composition.
In-memory success is never claimed as durable disk persistence or Keychain behavior.
exercise.solution:
This scratch implementation extends CardStore with an actor-owned dictionary. The async protocol lets outside callers await access to the actor, even though its replacement method performs one synchronous state change. Nothing waits halfway through replacing an account entry. That protects the in-memory transition; a disk transaction and its failure policy would be separate work.

actor MemoryCardStore: CardStore {
    private var cardsByAccount: [String: [StoredCard]] = [:]

    func read(for accountID: String) throws -> [StoredCard] {
        try Task.checkCancellation()
        return cardsByAccount[accountID] ?? []
    }

    func replace(_ cards: [StoredCard], for accountID: String) throws {
        try Task.checkCancellation()
        cardsByAccount[accountID] = cards
    }

    func clear(for accountID: String) throws {
        try Task.checkCancellation()
        cardsByAccount[accountID] = nil
    }
}

struct CardFeatureDependencies: Sendable {
    let accountID: String
    let store: any CardStore
}

func syntheticDependencies() -> CardFeatureDependencies {
    CardFeatureDependencies(
        accountID: "synthetic-account-a",
        store: MemoryCardStore()
    )
}

Use try await store.replace(..., for: "synthetic-account-a"), then read A and B through the same protocol. Store a different card for B, clear A, and verify B survives. The protocol declares throws even though this fake has only cancellation-related failure; a durable implementation can report disk or schema errors without changing all consumers.

The memory fake equates an absent account entry with an empty collection. That is acceptable for this exercise's contract, but a cache requiring “never loaded” versus “loaded empty” needs a separate optional or freshness record. Replacing a collection is atomic with respect to this actor's in-memory state; it does not establish transaction durability on disk.

A disk-backed worked design would encode a schema-versioned envelope, write to an appropriate account-scoped path with an atomic replacement policy, select protection and backup behavior, and preserve distinct read/write failures. A credential adapter instead uses Keychain identities and OSStatus handling. Keep those adapters separate. Finally, pair logout clearing with invalidation of pending repository work so an old request cannot refill A after this store clears it.
