lessons.title: Data lab: accept only the right account and request
lessons.summary: Build a fakeable card repository with an account cache. Use exact request ordering to prove that old responses cannot replace current data.
objectives: Write the repository's behavior in words before writing its implementation.
Keep endpoint-shaped DTOs separate from safe domain snapshots.
Reject old successes after an account change or newer request.
Use fakes with controlled start and finish events to check failure order and cache behavior.

sections.title: Write what a caller should see
sections.html:
A repository gives callers one agreed way to load and cache data. Think of an Android repository joining Retrofit with a memory cache while a ViewModel displays the current account's cards. Start with its behavior, not its class name. This scratch iOS repository loads made-up cards, saves successful snapshots, supports forced refresh, and preserves cancellation. A snapshot is a value describing data at one moment. The repository must reject old successful answers from a previous account or an earlier request.

Write the contract in ordinary language: the cache is memory-only and account-scoped; cached reads return the current successful snapshot; forced requests bypass that cache; a refresh failure preserves the previous snapshot but throws to the caller; only the latest started network request for the current account may commit. A superseded result is a distinct error, not an empty success. Changing account clears the cache and invalidates outstanding results.

This latest-started policy has a consequence: if a newer request fails, an older request still cannot install its later success. Another product might prefer newest successful response or explicit coalescing. Those are different policies, so choose and test one. Do not let task scheduling accidentally choose your product behavior.

The lab uses no real account, endpoint, database, or token. Build it in a scratch target. The course presents a worked design for comparison, while leaving you to create and run the practice implementation.

sections.title: Give each layer one decision to make
sections.html:
A boundary separates responsibilities. Here the remote adapter builds requests, uses the approved transport, checks status, decodes DTOs, and returns domain values. The repository owns its cache and request versions. Presentation owns the current screen request, loading display, and quiet handling of cancellation or replacement. The account networking layer owns credentials. A DTO is shaped for the endpoint; a domain snapshot is shaped for the caller. Separate these decisions so each test can focus on one promise.

Define a small LabRemote: Sendable protocol with an async throwing fetch method, and use immutable LabCard values. Do not pass a dictionary of Any or a live database object across actors. A fake implementing the same protocol can pause a response until the test releases it. A production adapter would use session 018's pipeline rather than constructing an unconfigured session in the repository.

The returned snapshot includes account identity, not just cards. That helps presentation verify that it still belongs to the screen's current account. It does not authorize logging that identity or any real user data. In the lab all identifiers are synthetic.

Do not add DI resolution inside fetch or load. Supply the remote implementation once during construction. The composition root then makes lifetime and substitution reviewable. A protocol does not need a container to be useful; a direct initializer is sufficient for this experiment.

sections.title: Save two numbers before waiting
sections.html:
A generation is a version of account ownership. A request number identifies which network load started most recently. Save both inside the repository actor before awaiting the remote fetch. Waiting gives another operation a turn: it might start a newer request or change the account. After the fetch succeeds, compare both saved numbers with current state. The first check asks “same account period?” The second asks “still the latest load?” The actor protects access to the numbers, while the comparisons protect their meaning.

Use separate counters because cache invalidation and request replacement have different meanings. Increment the account generation when account ownership resets, even if the textual account ID later becomes the same again. An A-to-B-to-A sequence must not allow an original A response to appear current merely because the string matches.

After fetching, first preserve cancellation, then reject stale ownership, then reject supersession, then commit the immutable snapshot. Keep that final commit synchronous on the same actor. If you add an awaited disk write between validation and commit, actor reentrancy creates another interval to reason about. A separate store may need its own compare-and-commit generation contract.

Cancellation is still useful for resource efficiency. The guards remain necessary when the fake, transport, or server completes despite cancellation. Never present a successful cancellation test as proof that stale ownership cannot occur.

A failed remote call exits through the catch path, so it needs a cancellation check there too. If the caller was canceled and a fake later throws offline, Task.checkCancellation() makes caller cancellation win. If the caller is still active, rethrow the original remote error. Do that even if the account or request number changed. No failed result is cached. In this contract, accountChanged and superseded classify successful responses that arrived too late; they do not replace ordinary remote failures.

sections.title: An empty answer is still an answer
sections.html:
A cache is a saved copy you can reuse. In this lab, a missing cached snapshot means no successful load has been saved. A snapshot containing zero cards means a load succeeded with an empty answer. Represent the cache as an optional snapshot so these states remain distinct. Testing isEmpty alone would treat a valid empty result as a miss and fetch again. The successful empty snapshot should be reusable until the lab's stated refresh or account-change rule invalidates it.

The lab has no TTL: cached values stay usable until explicit refresh or account change. That limitation is acceptable because it is stated. A production freshness contract should record fetched time or server validation metadata and inject a clock for testing expiry. Use monotonic time for elapsed durations; use wall-clock time when persisted timestamps or server dates require it. Those clocks are not interchangeable.

If a refresh fails, the previous snapshot remains stored, but the call throws. Presentation may show previous content plus a retry state. Returning old data as if it were freshly fetched would hide the failure. A richer return type could explicitly identify cached or stale content, but should not be introduced until the consumer needs it.

Eviction removes a cached value but lets work already running fill it again. Invalidation also changes the ownership generation, so older work cannot refill the new cache. The active AsyncCache documents that distinction. Account change needs the stronger invalidation rule. Inspect its tests to see what an old caller receives as well: rejecting a cache write is not necessarily the same as rejecting that caller's returned result.

sections.title: Control the order in your fake
sections.html:
A gate is a test-controlled pause. Build a fake remote actor that records a request's start and lets the test release its result. Start request A and wait for its start signal. Start B and wait for its signal. Release B, then A. The cache must contain B's value, and A must throw supersession: a newer request took its place. Short sleeps cannot guarantee this order. Keep start and finish signals explicit so the test proves the intended state change.

For account switching, start A's request, change to B, then release A. Assert the account-change error and an absent cache. Add A-to-B-to-A to prove identity equality cannot defeat generation checking. For cancellation, cancel the caller while its fake is paused, release it, and assert cancellation with no new commit. A fake should also be able to fail with an ordinary synthetic transport error.

Check cache hits by counting remote calls: the second non-forced read should reuse a successful snapshot, including an empty one. Check force by verifying another remote call starts. Check failed force refresh by verifying the old cache remains and the failure is observable.

Finally verify the remote adapter separately with session 018's HTTP fixtures. Repository tests should not become URLSession tests, and URLSession fixture tests should not need a view hierarchy. These boundaries make failures easier to localize and preserve realistic contracts.

Add three controlled error rows: cancel the paused caller then release an offline failure, expecting CancellationError; invalidate account ownership then release offline failure without canceling, expecting the original offline error and no cache refill; start B then fail A without canceling A, expecting A’s original remote error and no change to B. Also fail an active forced refresh after a cached success and assert the cache survives. These rows distinguish the two precedence paths instead of merely testing late successes. Use the explicit start/completion gates in SwiftLanguageLab as the host practice boundary; retain each request’s result for assertions.

sections.title: The screen must also check before displaying
sections.html:
Presentation is the code that chooses visible screen state. It has its own commit: accepting a returned snapshot onto the screen. A correct repository answer can become old while presentation waits. Record the screen's request identity before loading, then check it before assigning visible state. Also check that the snapshot belongs to the screen's current account. MainActor protects UI access, but allows other work to run during an await. The screen therefore needs a freshness rule as well.

If a synchronous button launches Task, retain and cancel its handle at the feature's defined stopping event. Alternatively let a framework-managed task call an async presentation method. Do not bury an independent Task inside every repository method; the caller already supplies an asynchronous lifetime and should see its errors.

For repository grounding, inspect the credential actor's logout-during-refresh test and AsyncCache's invalidation test. They demonstrate the same broad invariant with different business rules. Our lab rejects an old caller's result, whereas the generalized cache can return an old result while refusing to store it. Copying a helper without understanding that difference changes the feature contract.

Your lab handoff should include a short behavior table, the gated tests you ran, and the limits: memory-only persistence, no shared in-flight coalescing, no retry policy, and no real transport. Those limits identify the next design decisions without pretending this exercise is a completed production data layer.

quiz.question: Why track account generation as well as the account ID string?
options: Strings cannot be Sendable.
An A-to-B-to-A transition must still invalidate the original A request.
Generation encrypts account data.
quiz.explanation: The same textual account identity can represent a later ownership period. A monotonically changed generation rejects work started before an intervening reset.

quiz.question: A forced refresh fails while an older snapshot is cached. What does this lab promise?
options: It clears the old cache and returns empty success.
It retains the prior snapshot but throws the refresh failure.
It reports the old snapshot as freshly fetched.
quiz.explanation: Retaining usable content and reporting a failed refresh are compatible. The caller can show old content with a recovery state without hiding the failure.

quiz.question: Is an actor-protected repository enough to prevent stale UI updates?
options: Yes, all actors share one transaction.
No, presentation must validate its own request and account context before committing.
Yes, if the cards are Codable.
quiz.explanation: Repository and presentation have separate ownership boundaries. A screen can change while awaiting the repository even when the repository's internal commit is correct.

exercise.brief: Build the made-up card repository in a scratch target. Use a fake you can pause and release. Explain “latest started wins,” and mark every cancellation and ownership check.
steps: Create LabCard, LabSnapshot, LabRemote, and LabRepository in a scratch Swift target.
Pass in a fake remote. Let the caller own load's task instead of launching a separate Task inside load.
Support cached and forced reads. Keep separate account-generation and request-number counters.

acceptance: Only the latest started request in the current account generation commits.
Successful empty results are cached; failed refresh preserves an existing snapshot and throws.
Cancellation, account change, and supersession remain distinct outcomes.

The lab accurately declares memory-only storage and lack of coalescing.
exercise.solution:
The implementation below keeps cache checks and the final write in the same actor. After it checks the saved account and request numbers, it writes the snapshot without another await. No other repository operation can take a turn between those checks and that in-memory write. The remote call earlier in the method can wait, so it needs checks on both sides.

struct LabCard: Sendable, Equatable {
    let id: String
    let title: String
}
struct LabSnapshot: Sendable, Equatable {
    let accountID: String
    let cards: [LabCard]
}
protocol LabRemote: Sendable {
    func fetch(accountID: String) async throws -> [LabCard]
}
enum LabLoadError: Error {
    case accountChanged
    case superseded
}
actor LabRepository {
    private let remote: any LabRemote
    private var accountID: String
    private var accountGeneration = 0
    private var requestNumber = 0
    private var cached: LabSnapshot?

    init(accountID: String, remote: any LabRemote) {
        self.accountID = accountID
        self.remote = remote
    }

    func load(force: Bool = false) async throws -> LabSnapshot {
        try Task.checkCancellation()
        if !force, let cached { return cached }

        requestNumber += 1
        let startedRequest = requestNumber
        let startedGeneration = accountGeneration
        let startedAccount = accountID
        let cards: [LabCard]
        do {
            cards = try await remote.fetch(accountID: startedAccount)
        } catch {
            // Cancellation of this caller wins over an ordinary remote error.
            try Task.checkCancellation()
            // Without caller cancellation, retain the remote's original error.
            throw error
        }
        try Task.checkCancellation()

        guard accountGeneration == startedGeneration,
              accountID == startedAccount else {
            throw LabLoadError.accountChanged
        }
        guard requestNumber == startedRequest else {
            throw LabLoadError.superseded
        }
        let snapshot = LabSnapshot(accountID: startedAccount, cards: cards)
        cached = snapshot
        return snapshot
    }

    func changeAccount(to newAccountID: String) {
        accountGeneration += 1
        requestNumber += 1
        accountID = newAccountID
        cached = nil
    }

    func currentSnapshot() -> LabSnapshot? { cached }
}

The precedence has two explicit paths. After a successful remote return, caller cancellation wins, then accountChanged, then superseded, then success. If the remote throws, the catch checks caller cancellation first; otherwise it rethrows that original remote error, including a remote CancellationError. Account and request guards classify successful results only; they do not replace an ordinary failure with a stale-ownership error. The prior snapshot therefore survives a failed forced refresh. A cache hit does not start a new network request or supersede an existing refresh.

A deterministic worked scenario starts request one for synthetic account A, starts request two, releases two with card B, and then releases one with card A. The second call succeeds and cache inspection returns B; the first throws superseded. For an account-switch scenario, change to synthetic B before releasing A; the old result throws accountChanged and currentSnapshot remains nil.

To extend this toward durable storage, do not simply await store.replace after the guards. Define a store command carrying ownership generation, or centralize durable commit in an owner that validates that generation. To add coalescing, specify whether caller cancellation affects shared work and how each waiter stops. These are follow-on contracts, not missing annotations.

lessons.summary: Trace one real request path. Compare what callers observe before replacing an API, then plan a small migration with checks and a clear recovery limit.

sections.title: Review what each part promises
sections.html:
Architecture is how parts divide responsibility and work together. Your Android experience with features, use cases, repositories, and HTTP clients gives useful questions. Ask who owns state, errors, and work lifetime in this iOS path. UIKit navigation, Swift values, actors, and package targets may divide those jobs differently. A boundary is where one part makes a promise to another. Judge whether that promise is understandable and testable, rather than counting boxes or insisting on familiar layer names.

Start a review with a concrete behavior: a synthetic query becomes search parameters, a service executes the request, and a caller receives results. Trace a method in the active checkout rather than guessing from a similarly named older file. This repository contains duplicate-looking legacy paths; use the verified Projects sources and inspect imports, package targets, and callers to establish relevance.

For every boundary, record input, output, errors, isolation, lifetime, account context, and resource ownership. This is a compact contract inventory. A change from PromiseKit or a publisher to async/await can simplify control flow while still changing cancellation, timing, replay, or error delivery. A transport replacement can change cookies, interception, redirects, and tracing even if it returns identical bytes in one test.

The goal of this review is a defensible migration plan and a tested synthetic seam. It is not permission to edit production modules or claim a complete application migration.

sections.title: Follow calls to where objects are built
sections.html:
A declaration states what callers may ask; composition is where the app chooses the object that answers. Start with SearchServiceModule in ZDModules. Its MainActor rule, argument labels, async method, and thrown errors constrain the caller. Then inspect the feature converter's async let lookups and optional fallback. It resolves search inputs. Its name alone does not prove that it owns transport or the whole search workflow. Follow the concrete calls and construction sites to establish that path.

Follow networking into the request processor and dispatcher. The async processor prepares a request, participates in hooks and tracing, performs auth-aware request handling, and processes the response. The URLSession dispatcher receives an injected provider. Credential adaptation belongs to the credential provider, not the view model. These are observable responsibilities in named files; avoid claiming every operation follows precisely the same path without tracing its concrete dispatch mode.

Finally inspect app composition. It creates a configured session, wraps it in the interception provider, and supplies it as an alternate dispatcher. Application startup checks a flag and can enable that alternative. This establishes coexistence and a selection point; it does not tell you the production flag value for every user or prove that legacy dependencies are removed.

At each step distinguish compile-time dependency from runtime selection. A Package.swift dependency proves a target can import something, not that every running request uses that implementation. A comment is useful intent; a call site and test provide stronger behavioral evidence.

sections.title: Put knowledge where callers need it
sections.html:
A domain contract states a promise in the caller's own terms, such as search inputs and a result snapshot. UI code needs presentation state, navigation, and recovery choices. It usually does not need to build bearer headers or decode JSON. An adapter connects that domain promise to infrastructure details such as HTTP status or database access. Keep those details there when possible, and map failures into the boundary's agreed model. This makes the consumer's knowledge smaller and its responsibilities clearer.

That is a direction for design, not a claim that the checkout is a textbook clean architecture. ZDModules includes UIKit-facing contracts and dependencies. Some services are MainActor-isolated. Existing reactive and promise helpers carry legacy semantics. A good review identifies the actual seam that can improve without rewriting every consumer at once.

Ask whether each protocol has multiple meaningful consumers or an actual replacement boundary. An interface wrapping a single trivial pure function may add ceremony. Conversely, a concrete network client passed everywhere may expose too much configuration and ownership. Constructor injection and a narrow protocol can help when they isolate real variability or resource scope.

Check dependency direction at the package level. Shared contracts should not import concrete feature implementations merely to reuse a helper. Public model types increase the cost of future change. Avoid pushing request IDs, decoder strategies, and global DI containers into every API unless the consumer truly needs to control them.

sections.title: Compare behavior before replacing an API
sections.html:
Equivalence means the caller sees the same promised behavior. For a one-result operation, compare values, errors, cancellation, how many times completion happens, and when work begins. An async function returns one result. A publisher might deliver a cached value and then a fresh value. They cannot be swapped just because both load cards. A bridge can let callers move in small steps, but must state which behaviors it preserves or intentionally changes, including the owner of work and its stop rule.

For a stream, ask when production starts, how many readers it supports, whether old values replay, how much can be buffered, what may be dropped, and how production stops. A Task that sends to a subject can emit before a subscriber attaches. A checked continuation must resume exactly once, even if cancellation and completion arrive together. Protect that choice with synchronized state. An ordinary shared Boolean cannot safely settle the race by itself.

For transport, compare request configuration, cookies, headers, redirects, TLS and trust handling, interception, payload size, cancellation mapping, and trace propagation. The repository's configured alternate dispatcher is a better migration seam than introducing URLSession.shared in each feature. Preserve the established credential owner and its stale-completion checks.

Use synthetic fixture parity tests for observable contract behavior. Do not mirror private implementation steps in tests, and do not send real write operations through both implementations merely to compare them. Shadowing a side-effecting request can itself duplicate the operation.

sections.title: Choose what happens to requests already running
sections.html:
A route is the selected implementation for an operation. Snapshotting the route means saving that choice when the request starts. Later switches affect later requests; they do not redirect one already waiting. Drain-then-promote is different: wait for active requests to finish before using the new dispatcher. Choose the policy that matches shared session state and resource lifetime. The small gateway in this exercise snapshots each request's route. It does not track or drain active operations.

The checkout explicitly documents a drain-then-promote alternate-dispatcher strategy at startup and in request tracking. Read its state implementation and tests before promising the same behavior elsewhere. The worked gateway below only snapshots the route; it does not implement draining. Precise labels prevent a small experiment from being mistaken for the full production mechanism.

Define rollback at the composition boundary, not as a catch-all automatic fallback on every error. Retrying a failed write through another transport can repeat a server side effect. Even for reads, a fallback can hide genuine failures and distort metrics. A route switch for future requests is easier to reason about than replaying current operations without an idempotency contract.

Measure failure and cancellation separately, request duration, refresh count, active request count, and stream drop behavior. Use aggregate metadata without payloads, tokens, or sensitive identifiers. Define rollout stop conditions and an accountable owner before enabling a production flag; this lesson does not perform that enablement.

sections.title: Label facts, risks, and proposals
sections.html:
Evidence is something another engineer can inspect. Keep three kinds of statement clear. A source observation says “this adapter ends normally on publisher failure.” A suspected risk says “a caller expecting a thrown error may hide that failure.” A proposal says “use a throwing stream at this boundary.” The first is visible in code. The second depends on a caller's behavior. The third needs caller review and tests. Separating them helps a review stay accurate without pretending source inspection proved a production incident.

Do not describe annotations such as @unchecked Sendable as proof of safety. Identify the actual state protection, or record that it still needs inspection. Likewise, a Swift 6 compiler installed locally does not establish every target's language mode or isolation defaults. Effective build settings and package target configuration are part of migration evidence.

A useful handoff names the smallest seam, the behaviors preserved, intentional differences, fixtures checked, unverified areas, rollout mechanism, and rollback criteria. Avoid an unbounded “migrate the data layer” project when a single shared transport or stream adapter provides a concrete first step.

Finish by explaining one tradeoff you chose. A snapshot-per-request gateway is simpler than draining but leaves old requests active. Latest-state buffering limits memory but loses intermediate values. Account invalidation improves correctness but can turn an old caller into a canceled or stale outcome. Staff-level architecture judgment makes these consequences visible.

quiz.question: The app constructs an alternate URLSession dispatcher. What can you conclude?
options: All production traffic already uses URLSession.
There is a configured alternative and selection boundary; runtime usage still depends on routing.
The existing dispatcher can be deleted immediately.
quiz.explanation: Construction proves availability. The startup flag and state determine runtime selection, and coexistence does not establish complete migration or safe dependency removal.

quiz.question: A publisher emits cached data followed by fresh data. Is async throws -> Value an equivalent replacement?
options: Yes, both use asynchronous syntax.
No, the number and timing of values differ unless the contract is intentionally changed.
Yes, if Value is Sendable.
quiz.explanation: A one-shot function cannot preserve two separate deliveries without a new return model or stream. Equivalence includes timing, cardinality, failure, and cancellation.

quiz.question: Why avoid automatic fallback to the old transport after a write times out?
options: The old transport is always slower.
The server may already have committed the write, so replay can duplicate it.
Swift cannot express fallback.
quiz.explanation: A timeout creates uncertainty, not proof of no side effect. Fallback replay requires the same idempotency and retry reasoning as any repeated write.

exercise.brief: Review the checkout's request boundary without editing it. In a scratch target, make a route gateway for made-up reads. Propose one small change with behavior checks and recovery rules.
steps: Trace SearchServiceModule, request processing, credential ownership, alternate dispatcher construction, and startup selection.
At each boundary, record state ownership, lifetime, failure, account scope, and the source that supports your claim.
Make a gateway that captures its selected implementation before awaiting a made-up read.
Pause one fake read, switch selection, and release it. Check that only later reads use the new route.
Write the review with fixture coverage, intended differences, stop conditions, and production rollout facts you have not verified.
acceptance: Every claim about the checkout has a verified active file anchor.
The gateway preserves an in-flight request's chosen implementation.
The review distinguishes route snapshotting from draining and rollback from replay.
No existing client source, flag, credential, or live request is modified.
The proposal has a concrete scope and caller-visible acceptance criteria.
exercise.solution:
This scratch gateway keeps the selected route stable for one read. Its actor owns selection; its two readers follow one Sendable protocol. The method saves the chosen dependency before it waits. Another call to select can change future selection during that wait, but cannot change this method's saved dependency. The example proves route consistency for synthetic reads, not the checkout's full migration mechanism.

struct MigrationCard: Sendable, Equatable {
    let id: String
    let title: String
}
protocol MigrationReading: Sendable {
    func read(id: String) async throws -> MigrationCard
}
enum MigrationRoute: Sendable { case existing, alternate }

actor MigrationGateway {
    private var route: MigrationRoute = .existing
    private let existing: any MigrationReading
    private let alternate: any MigrationReading

    init(
        existing: any MigrationReading,
        alternate: any MigrationReading
    ) {
        self.existing = existing
        self.alternate = alternate
    }

    func select(_ newRoute: MigrationRoute) {
        route = newRoute
    }

    func read(id: String) async throws -> MigrationCard {
        try Task.checkCancellation()
        let selected: any MigrationReading
        switch route {
        case .existing: selected = existing
        case .alternate: selected = alternate
        }
        let result = try await selected.read(id: id)
        try Task.checkCancellation()
        return result
    }
}

A worked review would state: “Observed: app composition creates an alternate configured URLSession dispatcher, and startup can enable it. Proposed scope: test one read operation through both injectable providers with the same synthetic fixtures. Preserve status validation, cancellation, credential adaptation, interception configuration, and tracing. Do not change account ownership or replay failed writes. Rollback selects the existing implementation for future operations. Runtime flag exposure and device performance remain unverified.”

For the route test, start a read against an existing fake and hold it, select alternate, then release the existing fake. Its result must still come from existing. Start a second read and verify alternate receives it. If draining is required, add explicit active-operation tracking and tests for when promotion happens rather than renaming this gateway.

The learning gateway does not reproduce the real client's interception, retries, draining, or tracing. It isolates one correctness property so you can reason about it. A production proposal should attach the exact operation's fixture parity results and identify the composition owner before a rollout. This is a review artifact and synthetic experiment, not a completed migration.

simple.story: A courier office has two bicycle routes across town. Hana writes “river route” on parcel R1 before its rider leaves. The office then chooses the market route for future parcels. R1 is already out with its route card; it still comes back by the river route. Parcel R2, sent afterward, uses the market route. Changing the office's choice is simple when each parcel keeps its starting choice. Waiting for every rider to return before switching would be another policy, with different tracking and waiting rules.
simple.meaning: A migration gateway can capture the selected dependency before awaiting it. This preserves each request's route. The checkout's documented drain-then-promote strategy is a separate, stronger mechanism.

example.change: Select alternate, release R1, and then start read R2.
example.after: R1 still returns the existing fake's value. R2 uses alternate. Selecting alternate did not cancel, drain, or replay R1.
